To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a brief intervention to reduce substance use during pregnancy is feasible to administer and acceptable to participants.

1) a brief computer-based intervention can increase abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana among pregnant women and reduce their risk-taking behavior in the context of sex, 2) the intervention was more effective for women with high baseline substance use and risky sex behavior, 3) it was more effective for African American women and women who had a history of substance use and risky sexual behavior, and 4) it was more cost effective than standard care.

(a) a brief intervention delivered via computer to women who use alcohol and/or drugs during pregnancy is effective in reducing substance use and risky sex; (b) the intervention was acceptable to the women and was not associated with any adverse events; and (c) the intervention was cost-effective.

the development of an intervention for substance use and risk-taking behaviors in pregnancy.
the effects of social and cultural factors on the health of women and children.
